May I also just say, that if you want to convince people of something, it's probably not good to start with calling them "fucking idiots", even if you have good arguments.

This is about spreading knowledge, and the kind of people who are most likely to blunder into some kind of real trouble (eg, with things beyond the scope of this sub) are exactly the kind of people for whom "Do not post any non-https links my fine gentlemen" would be meaningless noise to be ignored. How many people reading this thread did not know even this small tidbit about what plain HTTP exposes that HTTPS does not? I'd wager 95% of them.

Let's say that one day you, me, or someone else here amounts to something, and starts operating on the level where the rules are a little blurrier, and someone with access to your entire life's unencrypted browsing habits is on the other side of an issue that they care about. Or some day someone leaks some logs that tie your identity to http://image-hosting-site.com/jailbait-and-terrorism, and you have to spend the rest of your life hoping nobody you care about googles your name.

Frankly, you should be reading the news, looking at cat pictures and checking your email using HTTPS. Why I Am Not a Maker

I think what the author really has an issue with is materialism, which is maybe as common to people who identify as consumers (the types who make consumption a fashion) as it is to people who identify as producers. But I'll bet there are a lot of people who identify as "makers" who do it more out of love than financial interest. Lord knows you can get a bike flasher cheaper from China than you could ever make on your own but it's not for materialistic reasons that we might build a bike flasher. A lot of it is about discovery and creative expression, which I think the author does value. I wish the author had identified that distinction because it's not fair to put all "makers" under that umbrella, especially when there's a vague charge of sexism that goes with it.

Maybe there ought to be a subclass of "creators" that while they create artifacts of their work, don't necessarily do it for materialistic reasons. They might make flower pots, songs, or algorithms, all of which are artifacts but none of which are produced for materialistic reasons.

Although I have to admit I do feel like creating things makes you a superior to those who consume things. Not because it has material value but because it's a voice, sort of a proof you have a soul. The author is already an expert witer. Having talent like that and relegating yourself to being strictly a consumer or a curator or a critic, man that is no way to live in my very humble but honest opinion.

I live in Illinois. I have a product developer who I hired about 9 months ago lately has been non responsive to my inquiries. I have tried various methods of communications phone (goes to VM), email, and text messages. Am I being too paranoid or being too impatient? Do I need to take any legal actions? I am getting worried.

Any agreement has a "time for performance" term whether explicitly stated in the agreement or incorporated from local contract law. They have a deadline, everyone does. Try to figure out what that is and if past the deadline, demand your completed project in writing.

If before the deadline or unknown, you still have a right to "assurance of performance" if you suspect the other party's unwillingness to uphold their end of the bargain. You don't have to sit and wait forever for nothing to happen. Upon failure to provide adequate assurances you can cancel and seek damages for repudiation (usually a refund).

Depending on the amount of money at issue you may need to seek professional help. Contract law is old and complicated - think dating someone with two abusive ex's kind of complicated. So if you aren't willing to let the deal crash and walk away with nothing then buy a local lawyer for an hour and get some hard advice. Your wallet will thank you.
